deltas.delta: Correction to cycle 36: the arm64 reth-bsc binary carries two CRYPTOGAMS Keccak copies. The one that the Rust code calls is 'Keccak-1600 absorb and squeeze for ARMv8, CRYPTOGAMS by @dot-asm' with its round constants at file offset 0x3fe3540 (SHA3_absorb at 0x3fe3920 with 54 BL callers, SHA3_squeeze at 0x3fe3b00 with 40). The table at 0x3e8c240 that cycle 36 named belongs to a second routine, 'Keccak-1600 permutation for ARMv8, CRYPTOGAMS by appro@openssl.org', which has one caller. The SHA3 extension variants (_cext) have no BL caller.

cleared.check: L-1292: the Keccak-256 path of the arm64 reth-bsc v0.1.4-hotfix image, run from its machine code. A Python A64 model (a64sha3.py) decodes raw instruction words of SHA3_absorb, SHA3_squeeze, KeccakF1600 and KeccakF1600_int (312 distinct instructions, 15 classes, PAC hints as identity) and refuses any other instruction; hashes are formed as the Rust wrapper does, with the padding step in Python.
cleared.result: 5,077 permutations and 26,401 Keccak-256 values equal a reference checked against hashlib SHA3-256 and the empty-input Keccak-256: lengths 0 to 1,100, every rate boundary 136k-2 to 136k+2 for k up to 8, 560 inputs at byte offsets 1 to 7, 3,300 PoolManager key shapes (PoolKey 160 bytes, position key 58 bytes, transient delta key, mapping and nested mapping slots of ticks, bitmap, positions and ERC-6909 balances) and 22,000 bulk 32 and 64 byte inputs. Five planted faults (three round constant bits, one rotate amount, one lane count compare) were all caught. A validator on this image computes the same pool ids, slots and delta keys as geth validators. The Rust padding, buffer and cache code of the arm64 build and the byte-wise tail of SHA3_squeeze were not run.

leads.question: Run the arm64 reth-bsc Rust wrapper around SHA3_absorb and SHA3_squeeze (padding, partial block buffer, keccak_cache_global lookup) from the shipped machine code, as cycle 35 did for amd64.
leads.why: Only the CRYPTOGAMS routines ran this cycle. A platform-specific fault in the wrapper or cache would make an arm64 validator disagree with geth validators, which halts consensus and needs no ordinary account, so it stays operator level.

leadResults.answer: replay_sp.py in the work directory reads each pool's spacing from its Initialize log and tries only that spacing. 75 Polygon multi-step swaps replay to the unit: 25 of this cycle and the 50 of cycles 15 and 28 that had been recorded as failed because the endpoint refused state. Their spacings are 1, 4, 5, 10, 25, 60 and 200, all in replay.py's fixed list, so no earlier failure came from the list. The BNB Chain and Avalanche log queries returned nothing (range limits, and F-142 on publicnode), so the fixed list was used there and all 25 BNB Chain and 7 Avalanche samples replayed; the older BNB Chain windows of cycles 15 and 28 had already replayed in their own cycles and publicnode no longer serves their state.

The arm64 image's hashing routines ran from its machine code in an A64 model: 5,077 permutations and 26,401 Keccak-256 values over the theme's lengths and PoolManager shapes match, with 5 of 5 planted faults caught. Cycle 36 had named the wrong table: the routine revm calls is the @dot-asm 'absorb and squeeze' copy at 0x3fe3540, not the appro@openssl.org permutation at 0x3e8c240, which also matches. The Rust wrapper and cache on arm64 were not run and a new low priority lead records that. The hazard was operator level either way.
